analytic.title: Towards Dynamic Real-Time Latency Bounds in 5G Communication

div.p: Wireless systems require strict latency bounds for safety-critical applications, particularly in dynamic environments involving moving user equipment (UE) such as autonomous vehicles. Solutions in 5G mainly focus on static scheduling approaches in that regard, making them inapplicable for dynamic environments. However, latency in these dynamic settings is often unpredictable, creating a real challenge, as the need for safety is increased for moving systems, while at the same time, it is more challenging to ensure. Existing approaches typically detect latency violations after they occur, which is insufficient for realtime responsiveness, as it delays the reaction of UEs.

This paper proposes a novel method to predict latency in 5G wireless communication before transmission, enabling proactive safety measures. Our approach proposes modeling of resource scheduling from a real-time perspective to apply analytical latency calculation. We introduce formulas for predicting latencies for future time intervals and discuss how to determine bandwidth relevant to latency in 5G communication. The accuracy of our latency predictions thus is dependent on forecasting the available bandwidth and traffic load. However, our studies using realworld data show that our approach results in high precision, as 95.93% of our predictions match the experienced delay, making our solution applicable for real-world deployment.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: 5G aims to provide significantly lower latency than previous generations. It is expected to deliver ultra-low latency of a few milliseconds [1], which is essential for applications requiring real-time responsiveness, such as autonomous vehicles, remote surgery, and virtual reality. Safety-critical communication requires that deadlines are always met to prevent harm to the environment, particularly with moving user equipment (UE) such as autonomous driving vehicles. At the same time, the data rate available for safety-critical applications is limited and the increase in autonomous safety-critical systems in the future will lead to higher traffic loads [2], thus, challenging the validity of latency bounds in dynamic systems.

The primary problem addressed in this paper is the unpredictable latency in wireless networks, especially in dynamic environments involving moving UEs. Currently, safety violations are identified by detecting missed packets after the deadline [3], [4], which is a reactive approach [5].

The goal of this work is to proactively predict latency in wireless communication before transmission rather than detecting latency violations after they happen. By predicting latency violations, autonomous driving systems can trigger safety routines, such as slowing down or informing the user, earlier, thereby increasing overall safety. The proposed solution involves modeling the application requirements, the available resources, and the scheduling to predict latency bounds in real-time.

Our contributions include discussing how bandwidth relevant for latency can be determined in 5G wireless communication and, thereupon, introducing formulas for predicting latency in future intervals. The accuracy of these predictions depends on the quality of the forecast of available bandwidth. We evaluate our approach using real-world data to demonstrate its effectiveness. As a result, our methodology can significantly increase safety in future 5G applications.

The paper is structured as follows: Section II discusses the main idea of our approach in an example use-case, introducing the main benefits. Section III covers the system model with the key concepts of 5G relevant for later latency analysis. Section IV introduces means of predicting channel quality and defines our approach for deriving latency bounds in 5G. Section V follows with an evaluation of our approach on realworld test data. Finally, Section VI describes related work, and Section VIII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. USE-CASE
div.p: In wireless communication, the constantly changing environment, communication partners, and conditions lead to fluctuating Quality of Service (QoS). Current methodologies typically involve measuring latency or monitoring timestamps from received packets, which only allow retrospective evaluation of QoS. This delay in detecting deadline violations can have significant effects in safety-critical applications.

To address this, we introduce the concept of dynamic latency bounds that consider the dynamic nature of the communication environment. Our model, detailed in Sections III and IV, enables real-time derivation of latency bounds for communication between UEs and next-generation Node Bs (gNodeBs) using 5G in both directions. By dynamically modeling traffic load and channel conditions, and applying analytical methods for backlog and maximum delay estimation, we provide online (real-time) predictions of potential deadline violations. This proactive approach allows us to identify and mitigate risks before they result in safety-critical failures.

Connected driving services demand stringent reliability and low latency, requirements that intensify with higher levels of automation. Organizations such as 3GPP, ETSI, and 5GAA advocate using 5G networks with Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) deployments to support these services [6], [7]. The integration of 5G is expected to enable advanced Vehicle-toeverything (V2X) services via Vehicle-to-Network-to-Vehicle (V2N2V) communications, as highlighted in [8].

Cellular networks currently connect millions of vehicles through infotainment and telematics services, with expectations for exponential growth [2]. Leveraging existing cellular modems in connected cars offers significant financial and time-to-market advantages, particularly for Cellular Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) services. These solutions also support integration with smartphones and portable devices, enhancing protection for vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists [8]. Systems already planning to use V2N2V include the Safer Transport for Europe Platform (STEP), the Australian connected vehicle trial with Telstra and Lexus [9], the EU-funded NordicWay projects [10], and the Talking Traffic program in the Netherlands [11]. These initiatives aim to enhance road safety and efficiency through advanced communication technologies, thus, all of them require methods to provide bounds for the latencies in the network.

In the context of 5G communication, we define applications as specific communication use cases that leverage 5G technology to meet particular needs [1]. Example applications in automotive scenarios include collision avoidance and cooperative driving, and for smart factory operations sensor data exchange and emergency halts [12]. For safety-critical communication, current methods for detecting deadline violations observe missing acknowledgments or periodic heartbeat messages before a specified timeout [3], [4]. When deadline violations exceed the application's reliability requirements, safety or emergency routines are activated. These routines may involve sending alerts to the driver in semi-autonomous systems, relying more on local sensors such as LIDAR, radar, and cameras, increasing the following distance, reducing speed, or changing lanes to provide more time to react. Additionally, conservative driving strategies are prioritized, and emergency protocols may be initiated.

Figure 1 illustrates V2N2V communication for collision avoidance (CA) at intersections. In CA applications, vehicles share sensor data and driving intentions with nearby vehicles and infrastructure. Messages are sent periodically every 10 ms, with a maximum latency requirement D CA of 10 ms [1]. Thus, in Fig. 1b, messages are sent at the timestamps t 0 , t 1 , t 2 . If a message is not received before its deadline, a missed deadline is detected at t 4 . Our dynamic delay bounds d(t) change over time t and thus allow for prediction instead of detection. This results in time advantage to trigger safety reactions at two possible stages: 1) when the vehicle sends CA information (V2N) if the predicted latency exceeds 10 ms (d(t) > D CA ) at time t 2 , or 2) when the gNodeB shares this information with other vehicles (N2V) if the transmission time exceeds the remaining communication time (d(t) > D CA -∆t where ∆t is the time passed since sending from the vehicle, e.g., t 3 -t 2 ) at time t 3 . Thus, in this scenario, our approach can detect violations up to 10 ms before they occur, allowing vehicles to adopt defensive driving behaviors in advance. Assuming two cars approach each other with a relative speed of 70 km/h, they approach each other by 20 cm every 10 ms. For CA and other safety-critical applications, these distances are essential. We can see that predicting the latency does not reduce the system's safety, as deadline violations can still be detected traditionally after the period has passed. But it provides additional safety by allowing for earlier reactions. However, to ensure that the vehicle does not react too cautiously, the pessimism of the bounds should be as small as possible.

Furthermore, certain applications, such as emergency trajectory alignments, do not follow a periodic transmission pattern. Consequently, verifying whether the required latency guarantees are met under current conditions is challenging and typically requires the transmission of measurement messages, which increases network load. Our new approach addresses this issue analytically, ensuring continuous evaluation of latency requirements without additional network traffic.

Future applications may require an interface for demandbased latency evaluation, offering Quality on Demand (QoD) for critical applications. Thus, our models could be integrated in gNodeBs to allow for dynamic adjustments in load, delaying or dropping less critical packets during critical situations. This requires highly performant models for fast evaluation, ensuring sufficient but not excessive adaptations.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: Our system operates using the current traffic load at a given time instance while predicting the service rate for 5G, a method that will be detailed in the following sections. Based on the predicted service rate and given load, we then determine the expected latency, which will be explained in Section IV.
In this section, we show how the 5G New Radio (5G NR) physical layer can be simplified to only a few parameters within the context of a Response Time Analysis (RTA).

In 5G NR communication, channel resources are defined in the frequency and time domains. Dedicated channel bandwidths are allocated to the so-called ITS domain to separate critical vehicular communication from other domains, such as regular mobile communication. Within those channels, vehicles communicate with other vehicles via the network infrastructure (cf. V2N2V communication in Figure 1a). Available cellular V2X channels are 5895 MHz to 5925 MHz in the US [13] and 5855 MHz to 5925 MHz in the EU [14]. Both bandwidths are split into channels of 10 MHz to 20 MHz, with the larger overall bandwidth in the EU further divided between Wi-Fi and cellular communication. Here, the channels in the EU are technology-neutral. Larger channels by frequency support higher data rates, targeting data-intensive applications, while smaller ones can protect critical applications with lower data demands. However, the overall bandwidth limitation to either 30 MHz (US) or at most 70 MHz (EU) imposes a hard limit for the available data rate. The bandwidths associated with mmWave frequencies have not yet been released for the V2X domain, as they depend on short-distance and line-ofsight conditions, which are very vulnerable to interference [15]. Next, we will examine resource scheduling in V2X channels and simplify it to a basic model suitable for RTA of application data communication. The physical layer resource allocation principles of 5G NR are standardized in the ETSI TS 138 214 [16].In the time domain, 5G NR specifies a frame as an interval of 10 ms, further divided into subframes of 1 ms. In the frequency domain, the channel bandwidth is divided into subcarriers of 15 kHz, 30 kHz, or 60 kHz using Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiple Access (OFDMA). This flexible Subcarrier Spacing (SCS) in 5G NR allows for adaptable transmission durations of symbols. The minimum unit for allocating channel resources is a slot, which is a fixed transmission unit of 14 Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM) symbols. As depicted in Figure 2, a slot transmission takes a shorter time with a larger SCS. At 15 kHz SCS, the slot time is 1 ms, whereas it is reduced to 0.5 ms when doubling the SCS to 30 kHz. results in 168 OFDM symbols per PRB (14 symbols per slot x 12 subcarriers). We can conclude that choosing different SCSs does not affect the overall data rate. Rather, the shorter slot durations compensate for the increased bandwidth demand of a higher SCS. For example, if two 15 kHz PRBs are allocated in parallel, they can allocate the same resources as two 30 kHz PRBs allocated sequentially. Depending on the latency demands, flexible SCSs can be allocated into the resource grid of 5G NR (cf. Figure 3). Based on the assumption of a fixed number of symbols per time and a stable utilization of those available symbols, the data rate depends on the channel quality. The Shannon-Hartley-Law provides an upper bound to the available channel capacity based on the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and the channel bandwidth. While the channel bandwidth is fixed to the standardized channels, the signal strength emitted by the sender cannot be increased, due to regulations. Thus, the channel's capacity depends on the signal strength at the receiver, which is influenced by factors such as line-of-sight, the distance between sender and receiver, or fading effects like reflections or Doppler shift. To maximize the achieved utilization of the channel, the number of information bits per symbol must be optimized for the fixed number of symbols per PRB. This is done via the Modulation and Coding Scheme (MCS), which adjusts the redundancy per symbol to the respective SNR. The different MCS configurations are provided in Table 5.1.3.1-1 of ETSI TS 138 214 V16.2.0 [16]. Generally, the number of information bits per OFDM symbol N symb.
info is given by:
div.formula: N symb. info = Q m • r code 1024(1)
div.p: Here, Q m is the number of bits per symbol corresponding to the chosen modulation order (2 bits (QPSK), 4 bits (16 QAM), or 6 bits (64 QAM)). r code describes the coding rate, which is the number of information bits within 1024 transmitted bits.
In sum, the number of information bits per symbol should relate to the SNR in a way that maximizes spectral efficiency.
To obtain the overall data rate R ch (N symb. info ) of, for example, a 10 MHz channel, we can assume a given N symb.
info that optimally fits the current channel quality. Since the SCS does not change the number of symbols per second, we can determine the overall channel data rate using an exemplary SCS of 15 kHz:
div.formula: R ch (N symb. info ) = 10 MHz 15 kHz • 1000 slot s • 14 symbol slot • N symb. info (2)
div.p: For RTA, the worst-case execution time of an application data frame transmission is relevant. Following the above considerations, when an application i sends a data frame of size S frame , it then takes the fixed execution time C i as follows:
div.formula: C i = S frame R ch (N symb. info )(3)
div.p: In 5G NR data transmissions can aggregate PRBs in parallel, allowing the full channel data rate to be used. This approach enables priority mapping within a homogeneous resource, where frame transmission times follow each other. Due to the application data to resource block mapping, response times only need to be rounded up to at least the next full slot length. Since this work proposes an approach that improves safety via the prediction of data transmission time delays, frame loss is still managed by the given 5G NR V2X reliability mechanisms within the above-modelled communication. Here, for example, the standard reliability mechanisms of blind retransmissions can be applied to Equation (3) by doubling the application frame size S frame .

div.head: IV. METHODOLOGY
div.p: In the context of mobile and highly dynamic applications, such as V2X communication, having a method which computes online a worst-case delay for applications is crucial. The aim of our work is to determine latency in real-time which results in a continuous re-evaluation in case of changes in network conditions. The accuracy of the channel estimation plays an important role in the performance of the wireless communication systems and, in our case, for the latency bound computation. In this section, we define the most adopted solutions for channel quality prediction, followed by some details regarding the currently used analytical model for RTA.

div.head: A. Forecasting Solutions for Dynamic Channel Conditions
div.p: One recurrent approach for channel estimation with good performance is the use of deep learning techniques. The authors in [17] are capable of learning long-term dependencies. A special architecture allows the LSTM model to decide whether to retain previous information in short-term memory or discard it. For more details about LSTM, see [17].

Another very popular algorithm for forecasting a time-series of non-stationary data is the Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model [18]. It consists of three components: the autoregressive part AR(p), the integrated part I(d), and the moving average part M A(q). AR(p) considers the past q values of the series which are used in the prediction model. I(d) is used to make a time series stationary a degree of differencing d. The M A(q) component implies the error of the model in terms of q previous error terms. To create an ARIMA model, the most important process is to choose the appropriate order p, d, and q of the model. The authors of [19] demonstrate that ARIMA is able to predict accurately the network throughput with a percentage of errors, (i.e. the ratio of difference of predicted and actual value to the actual value) ranging from 0 to 4%. Similarly to LSTM, ARIMA can predict future data with a considerable accuracy level. [20] compares the accuracy of ARIMA, LSTM, and a standard linear regression which is a statistical model that fits the best line to the input data. The comparison is done in terms of Relative Error (RE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). MAE captures the error in the absolute prediction and RE represents the fraction of the error in the prediction with respect to actual channel variation.

div.head: B. Response Time Analysis
div.p: Variations in channel quality influence the MCS applied by the base station to the current transmission and consequently, it leads to an increase or decrease in the overall throughput (see Eq. 1). In the context of RTA, to bound the worst-case latency, we reflect changes in MCS on changes in the transmission time of individual packets. Note that two packets with the same size can have different transmission times depending on the modulation scheme since it determines the number of bits per symbol Q m . Thus, the accuracy of the forecasting method for channel quality prediction plays a fundamental role in evaluating QoS in 5G wireless communication. By exploiting ARIMA and/or deep learning models we can formalize an analytical method for providing a worst-case latency bound. In our previous work [21] we show that considering static worst-case bound in systems which are highly dynamic results in highly pessimistic bounds. Thus, we introduced latency guarantees for differing contexts to better capture dynamic effects. According to [22], a context is any information that can be used to characterize a situation. We extended the notion of context-based on the environment of operation, considering variations in channel quality. A context Φ ∆t is characterized by an initial MCS value and a prediction model which estimates several cycles of channel degradations and improvements in that context over ∆t. First, consider a single application performing multiple data transmissions. Let C ′ i,Φ (q) be the transmission time of q packets from application i in context Φ. It is defined as:
div.formula: C ′ i,Φ (q) = C init i,Φ (q) + ∆C + i,Φ (q) -∆C - i,Φ (q)(4)
div.p: where, C init i,Φ (q) is the transmission time of q packets considering initial MCS value, ∆C + i,Φ (q) is the delay of transmission considering degradation of channel condition in that context, ∆C - i,Φ (q) is the reduced transmission time due to an improvement of channel condition. For more information, the full analysis can be found in [21]. 5G manages different classes of services and their requirements by integrating them into a single physical communication network. Thus, based on the size of transmissions, the application requirements, and the modulation scheme, the network scheduler allocates dynamically the required number of PRB to be used by a given application. Whenever wireless channel condition changes (i.e., improves or deteriorates), the modulation scheme is modified thereby leading to a new allocation of PRB. When multiple applications are transmitting at the same time, the network scheduler is not able to serve simultaneously all applications. In our work, we assume Static Priority Preemptive (SPP) scheduling where preemption is done on slot level and the priority is defined by different levels of criticality or importance among all the applications. The scheduler allocates PRBs first to higher priority applications and then to the ones with lower priority. Based on that, timing interference occurs which leads to a delay for lower-priority applications. In the future, we would like to integrate other scheduling approaches like Round-Robin approaches or Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) scheduling. To bound the transmission latency of low priority applications in the presence of other interfering ones, we rely on the busy-window approach [23]. Let ω + i (q) be the q-event busy windows of application i, which describe the maximum time interval required to complete the transmission of q consecutive packets, taking into account network slicing under the SPP scheduler. Given the busy window, we assume the critical instant (i.e. all applications start to transmit simultaneously) at the start of every context, accounting for maximum interference from the higher priority application. The worst-case response time ω + i,Φ (q) in a given context Φ ∆t required for q transmissions from application i in the presence of interfering higher priority application j is defined as:
div.formula: ω + i,Φ (q) ≤ γ i + C ′ i,Φ (q)+ ∀j∈hp(i) C ′ j,Φ (η j (ω + i,Φ (q)))(5)
div.p: where γ i is the minimum time unit for channel resource allocation in a slot defined as 1 ms (see Section III). C ′ i,Φ (q) is the execution time of slice i in isolation given the context Φ, and C ′ j,Φ (η j (ω + i,Φ (q))) is the delay due to the transmission of η j (ω + i,Φ (q)) packets from other interfering applications in context Φ. The function η j (∆t) denotes for every application j the maximum number of transmissions issued within a time window ∆t. The busy window is a fixed point computation, where results from the previous iteration are used for computing the transmission latencies in the current one.

div.head: V. EVALUATION
div.p: Since our model derives bounds for the transmission latency, we studied its Quality of Prediction (QoP) to describe the accuracy and confidence levels of the worst-case predictions. In the following section, we discuss some of the results obtained in [24] with new observations regarding pessimism and accuracy levels. For this, pyCPA [25] is used as a tool that implements the proposed busy window RTA in the context of the Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA).

div.head: A. Real-World Data Set
div.p: For the evaluation of our analytical model, we compared the latency bounds of the computed context-based RTA and simulation results of the SAMUS 5G simulator [26] using ARIMA. We consider two applications with different priorities, in which several UEs are performing multiple data transmissions.

• Traffic of photovoltaic systems transmitting proportionally to solar activity [27]. This slice has the highest priority with packet size of 1500 B. • Electric Vehicle Charging (EVC) point communication [28]. This slice has the second higher priority with packet size of 1950 B.

We focus only on bounding the latency of EVC since the response time of packets from SG is equal to their basic execution time, considering no timing interference from other applications with lower priority which would cause additional delay. The network configurations are summarized in Table II. More detailed information regarding the considered use cases and scenario are in [21].

div.head: B. Worst-Case Latency Evaluation
div.p: The accuracy of our worst-case latency is quantified by the residual which is the difference between the predicted value and the actual value obtained with SAMUS. Figure 4 visualizes the residuals of each context Φ during one minute of simulation. Note that the residual is given as an integer value since each packet is scheduled within the subframe length of 1 ms. Figure 5 shows the residual distribution in percentage. For nearly 95.6% of the transmission time, the predicted latency bound coincides with the actual simulation value. The pessimism of our RTA is represented by values greater than zero. They represent only the 2% of the cases and in the worst case, our latency bound is 7 ms greater than the real one. For Residual Value Non-Computable Fig. 4: Residual values for each context Φ 0.66% of the times, we obtained negative residuals where our bounds could not identify latency violations. A possible reason for the underestimation can be explained by fast fading [29] dynamics of the radio environment as these are being captured from the measurement equipment. Each orange cross represents a context for which the worstcase latency could not be computed (i.e., non-schedulable contexts). This happens for 1% of the time due to the limitations of schedulability and convergence conditions of pyCPA in case the current channel quality is extremely low, thereby resulting in a highly loaded system.

div.head: VI. DISCUSSION
div.p: Our proposed approach introduces a novel method for predicting latency in 5G wireless communication, necessitating a thorough discussion of its benefits and implications.

When considering the practical deployment of our solution, several aspects need to be addressed. A key point is that latency predictions must be made locally at the UEs and gNodeBs, necessitating highly efficient calculations in terms of both computation time and energy consumption. Future work will aim to compare different worst-case models to optimize these calculations. Predictions must also be available locally to avoid additional overhead. Notably, our approach can be implemented without requiring changes to protocol logic or message formats, and it remains effective even in heterogeneous environments where not all entities may install the prediction mechanisms. Additionally, if a latency violation is detected at the gNodeB, UEs need to be informed. These warnings can be transmitted via the control channel, adding negligible load due to their small size. To enhance reliability, these messages can be transmitted multiple times.

The practical benefits for autonomous driving systems are significant. Early latency prediction can substantially improve the safety and reliability of these systems by allowing them to trigger safety routines-such as slowing down, stopping, or informing the user-before a deadline violation occurs. Importantly, our approach does not compromise safety even if predictions are incorrect, as current state-of-the-art mechanisms detect deadline violations only after they occur, which can still be employed.

Our solutions are compatible with global scheduling methods, since the scheduled frame communication can allocate the full channel bandwidth by aggregating a sufficient number of resource blocks in parallel. Hence, this approach also matches network slicing, as the channel bandwidth can be easily adapted to a slice's given (reduced) bandwidth over time. Limitations could be faced in semi-persistent scheduling in V2X applications since there is no central resource allocation entity, that can enforce specific aggregation schemes.

A direct limitation of our approach is due to the stochastic nature of wireless communication. While our latency models use worst-case analysis for given predictions, the actual worst case can be lower, and packet losses may still occur. Therefore, the latency results do present absolute guarantees. Additionally, our solutions mainly benefit applications with larger deadlines (e.g., 10 ms or more). For deadlines significantly shorter than this, the time distance between predicted and detected deadline violation is small, resulting in less advantage in terms of reaction time or distance saved. Future work will focus on improving prediction models and exploring additional wireless technologies to enhance the flexibility of our approach. Another area for future research is incorporating more detailed information into predictions, such as the extent of the deadline violation and the confidence level of the prediction. Additionally, we plan to investigate load-dropping strategies of non-critical frames, until safetycritical messages can keep their deadlines. This can thus result in improved scheduling, where safety-critical packets can be prioritized on demand, without reducing the performance of other applications unnecessarily.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORK
div.p: The importance of temporal guarantees for dynamic traffic is highlighted in [30], emphasizing the evolving environments and requirements for connected vehicles.

Online modeling of worst-case latency has been studied in [31], where deterministic Network Calculus (NC) models are adapted based on live measurements to derive delay and backlog bounds for dynamic systems. Although this demonstrates that guarantees can be calculated in real-time, the modeled system was a wired hardware-in-the-loop setup and the approach has shown to be overly pessimistic. Thus, we need to rely on alternative methods for our bounds. Another approach for dynamic traffic in wired networks is presented in [32], which restricts traffic before it exceeds a certain load to ensure critical traffic is served.

In the wireless domain, dynamic bounds have been studied in IoT networks [33], but these models assume latency is mainly affected by sending intervals, which does not apply to 5G. In automotive networks, a protocol for wireless reliable real-time communication of large data objects is proposed in [34], focusing on latency guarantees at stable MCSs-related data rates rather than dynamic environments.

In 5G, Nota et al. [24] compute a global worst-case response time based on variable packet loads using static priority scheduling, but the work is pessimistic due to the assumption of fixed channel conditions. Mathew et al. [35] use NC to analyze delay in mixed fronthaul and backhaul 5G networks, highlighting the need to re-evaluate delays in 5G due to temporal variations and dynamic human activities, which motivates our approach. Liu et al. [36] apply NC to model ALOHA systems in 5G, obtaining a probability distribution for guarantees by stochastically selecting from deterministic functions. Ma et al. [37] use stochastic NC, and Coll-Perales et al. [38] use queuing theory to analyze 5G latency. However, both rely on Poisson process arrivals, making them unsuitable for safety-critical dynamic environments with bursty traffic. The model in [39] estimates latency in wireless systems, but unlike our approach, they focus on nearly static channel conditions (i.e. data rates are set in a relatively small range of 100 and 300 kbps). Skocaj et al. [40] also aim to detect delay violations proactively but rely on stochastic modeling of average performance, making it unsuitable for real-time applications.

Other studies use queuing theory or worst-case analysis, like NC, for stochastic worst-case guarantees on backlog and delay [37], [41]. These approaches require detailed environmental modeling, such as deterministically bounding the number of nodes in the 3D area, and reflections or interferences of the communication, which results in high model complexity even in simple chain topology analysis [41], making them unsuitable for online evaluation, where the environment cannot be entirely modeled before transmission.

Existing work on dynamic contexts often leverages machine learning for predicting channels, traffic, states, and other performance indicators, see [42] for an overview. While our solution can also use the benefits of machine learning for predictions, the latency model itself does not require machine learning, but can be derived analytical for the given predictions. This adds a level of explainability to the system, as the latency analysis is based on proven methods which can be verified by experts.

The foundations of our work on dynamic latency bounds were introduced in [21], which presented context-based guarantees. This paper extends that work by providing an online, real-time approach to latency prediction, addressing the limitations of static and retrospective methods.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In conclusion, this paper addresses the critical issue of unpredictable latency in wireless networks, particularly in the context of safety-critical applications involving moving user equipment such as autonomous vehicles. The proposed solution emphasizes the importance of predicting latency before transmission, rather than relying on reactive measures that detect safety violations post-facto. By introducing methods to predict latency, autonomous systems can proactively engage safety routines, significantly enhancing overall safety.

We have demonstrated how bandwidth relevant for latency can be determined in 5G communication and introduced predictive formulas for future time intervals using analytical worst-case approaches. While the accuracy of these predictions is contingent on the quality of bandwidth forecasts, evaluations using real-world data showed the effectiveness and potential of our solution for improving safety in 5G applications. Our results indicate a high precision of our predictions, which are neither overly pessimistic nor overly cautious.

In the future, we aim to minimize runtime to apply our approach in highly dynamic scenarios, extend our methods to other 5G scheduling approaches and cellular technologies, and include the latency predictions to better match application requirements with resources. This could involve assigning dynamic priorities or delaying less time-critical traffic to meet all deadlines where necessary, and thus optimizing the communication for safety in the future.
